text: Given a reference to a node in a connected undirected graph, return a deep copy of the graph. Each node has an integer value and a list of its neighbors.

Thanks. Before I dive in, I'd like to clarify a few things. Just to make sure I'm understanding this correctly — deep copy means every node in the result is brand new, and the neighbor links point to the new nodes, not the originals. And since it's an undirected graph, there are cycles. Is that right?
Right. It's connected and has cycles.

The cycles are the crux. If I naively recurse — to copy a node I copy its neighbors, which copy it back — I loop forever. So I need a map from original node to its clone: copy each node once, and when I meet a node that's already mapped, reuse its clone instead of recursing again. Are there any constraints on the input size?
Up to a hundred nodes. Values are unique and between one and a hundred.

Good — unique values in a small range. I'll come back to that for the follow-up. Let me run through the example: a four-node square, one, two, three, four, and back to one. I clone node one, then two, then three, then four — and every edge back to an already-cloned node just reuses the map. Result: four new nodes wired the same way.

Hmm, let me think about this for a sec. A naive approach would be to recurse without tracking anything — but on a cyclic graph that never terminates. This problem reminds me of DFS with memoization. The memo is the original-to-clone map: it both avoids duplicates and breaks the cycles. That's O of V plus E.

Here's the plan. One: if the node is already in the map, return its clone. Two: otherwise create a copy and store it in the map right away. Three: recurse into each neighbor, append the returned clones to the copy's neighbors, and return the copy. Here, I'm using the map to keep track of which originals I've already cloned. One thing worth flagging — I store the copy before recursing. If I recursed first, a cycle A, B, A would reach A before it's mapped, clone it again, and loop forever. There's a trade-off here. Since values are unique and at most a hundred, I can swap the hashmap for a fixed array of a hundred and one slots indexed by value — constant size. I'll show both. Does this approach sound good, or would you rather I think of another way?
Sounds good. Code it up, and show me that follow-up.

Alright, let me code this up. The main version guards against an empty graph, then runs DFS with an unordered map from original to clone. One thing worth flagging — the line that stores the copy in the map comes before the neighbor loop; that ordering is what makes cycles terminate. For the follow-up, the only change is the map's type: a vector of a hundred and one pointers, indexed by value. To be precise, that makes the map constant size, but the recursion stack is still O of V. For a general graph you can't reach true constant space — any traversal must remember what it visited. Unlike a linked list, a graph has no next pointer to enumerate its nodes for free.

Let's dry-run the code with the example: the four-cycle, one, two, three, four, starting DFS at node one. The row that matters is the second call on node one — the back-edge from node two. Node one is already in the map, so it returns the existing clone instead of cloning again; that's what stops the cycle. Every later call into a mapped node reuses it the same way, so every original ends up with exactly one clone. That matches. Corner cases: a single node with no neighbors returns one new node with an empty neighbor list. An empty graph returns a null pointer, handled by the guard at the top.

Let me think about complexity here. The time complexity is O of V plus E — each node is cloned once, and each edge is walked once from each end. The space complexity is O of V for the map plus the recursion stack. In the worst-case scenario, a long chain makes the stack that deep. Oh, one more thing — the follow-up brings the map down to constant size using the value-indexed array, but the traversal stays O of V. And if values weren't unique or the range were huge, the array trick breaks, and I'd fall back to the hashmap keyed on the node pointer.

Nicely done. Three things stood out. You identified the map as both the dedup and the cycle-breaker, and stored it before recursing. You gave the constant-size map follow-up from the unique-value hint. And you were precise that true constant space is impossible for a graph, because traversal itself is O of V. Good work.
